# 16-pairio — sources

Back-test entry `16-pairio.yaml`: Pairio, a voice assistant that helps factory technicians fix broken machines (YC
Spring 2026, P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named
(the launch-era site is in German; its quotes are given in German, with the author's English in brackets). "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-04-21 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era where one
exists; anything later is marked as later).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Pairio – Fix broken equipment in factories faster", 2026-04-21 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Q18-pairio-fix-broken-equipment-in-factories-faster

- [FAQ] pairio.com FAQ, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com/faq/
- [REF] pairio.com customer reference (Knipping), read 2026-10-22; figures "supplied by Knipping" — https://pairio.com/customer-references/
- [SITE] pairio.com, read 2026-10-22 — https://pairio.com

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Maintenance technicians and operators who fix machines on the production line.
   [LYC] "Pairio helps technicians and operators resolve faults faster with voice AI." [YCP] "AI mobile app that helps
   factory technicians fix broken machines". → `roles[technician]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: the
   technician only (operators are named too, but the fix and the report are the technician's).

2. **What (the job).** Get the machine running again fast, and keep the fix for the next person.
   [LYC] "Unplanned equipment downtime costs global industries over $1.4 trillion every year – and the root cause isn't
   broken machines. It's broken knowledge transfer." [LYC] "With the average technician in the US now 50 years old,
   knowledge is literally walking out the door". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the machine, when it fails, and afterwards when the fix should be written down.
   [LYC] "When a machine fails, resolution speed depends almost entirely on whether the one guy who's seen this before is
   working that day"; "Valuable technical clues are buried somewhere across 400 pages of OEM manuals or locked in outdated
   software"; "After spending 6 hours getting the line back up, the last thing a technician does is sit down and write a
   detailed fault report to institutionalize their knowledge". [FAQ] "Fundamentals and practical ways to use Pairio in
   day-to-day maintenance work." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: machine breakdown`. Author's choice: the window
   {5, WORKING_DAYS} (a working-day rhythm) and Frequency 2 to 4 working days out of 5 -- daily for the team, not for
   each technician (header); Prevalence `p_80_100`.

4. **Which people.** Technicians at US plants that keep their own maintenance team.
   [LYC] "Ask: Can you introduce us to plant and maintenance managers at US manufacturing firms?" [WB] "Pairio richtet sich
   an Unternehmen mit eigener Instandhaltung - vom Mittelstand bis zum Konzern." [Pairio is for companies with their own
   maintenance, from mid-sized firms to groups.] → `context.segment`, `market: US`; the German plants are in the header.

5. **Who pays.** The plant; the maintenance manager chooses, the plant manager agrees.
   [LYC] "If you know anyone in plant operations or maintenance in US manufacturing we'd love to talk with them". [WB]
   quotes a "Meister & Abteilungsleiter Instandhaltung" [foreman and head of maintenance] as a user. → `persona.
   decision_maker: {role: manager}`; Buyer and payer tests "The plant manager" (listed with "The IT department"):
   author's choice, no source names who signs. Purchase friction's tested item, "Connecting it to SAP or Maximo": [FAQ]
   "including systems such as SAP, IFS, IBM Maximo, Oracle EAM Cloud, Hexagon, SharePoint, Outlook, and Asset API"; [WB]
   "Die genaue Anbindung hängt von Ihrer IT-Landschaft ab." [The exact connection depends on your IT landscape.] The IT
   security review and the plant-wide rollout sign-off are the author's. Commitment's step, "run a pilot on one
   production line": [REF] "A clearly scoped pilot creates evidence"; "Following a two-month pilot, the solution was
   integrated in four weeks." (later than launch; the launch-era site offers "Kostenlose Demo" [free demo]).

6. **Mechanism.** Ask by voice or photo; answers from the manuals and past repairs; speak the fix, get a report.
   [LYC] "Simply ask and instantly receive any available technical clue"; "Speak and let Pairio structure their learnings
   into reusable know-how"; "Use photos and videos to capture even more contextual knowledge". [WB] "Sprache, Foto oder
   Video rein - fertiger Bericht raus" [voice, photo or video in, finished report out]; "Pairio erkennt Fehlerbild,
   Maßnahmen, Ersatzteile und erstellt einen strukturierten Bericht." [Pairio recognises the fault, the actions, the spare
   parts and writes a structured report.] [YCP] "Users just take a picture of the broken machine and we search thousands
   of pages of manuals to find the right solution." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (a phone
   allowed at the machine — tested; manuals as files; quiet enough to speak) and Adoption friction (speak the fix when
   done — tested; photograph the fault first) are the author's, from the mechanism's own needs and [BLOG] ("tools that fit
   how technicians actually work, on mobile, in loud environments"). Relative advantage: shorter_time from [WB] "-25%
   MTTR", less_help_needed from [LYC]'s "the one guy who's seen this before"; the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price public; the cost is technician time.
   [WB] "Kostenlose Demo" and "Demo buchen" [free demo; book a demo], no price; [SITE] "Book a free demo", no price.
   → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $600 to $1,200 per technician a year is **the operator's reading** (about $50 to
   $100 a seat a month; header). Existing sacrifice, HOURS 150 to 300 of the breakdowns per technician a year: author's
   arithmetic -- 3 to 6 hours a week of a technician's time lost to hunting through manuals, waiting for the one person
   who knows, extra trips for tools and parts, and the report written afterwards, over about 50 working weeks; the scale
   is set by [LYC]'s "6 hours getting the line back up" and by [WB]'s "-25% MTTR" and "-80% Ablageaufwand" (the shares
   the company says it removes). The rate, $31 an hour, is [BLS] "$30.82 per hour" (May 2025 median), the author's
   stand-in. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [BLOG] "At a specialty manufacturer in Illinois, the maintenance team told me some shifts run with a single
   technician."; "The troubleshooting descriptions? Consistently useless. 'Reset machine.' 'Machine broken, fixed it.'
   'Called supplier.'"; "The work order says there's a problem with the injection molding machine. That's it. They show
   up, assess, go back for parts, come back again."; "When a conveyor goes down, every minute counts in a way that's
   directly visible to the customer."; "she'd watched a technician try to use ChatGPT out of desperation to solve a
   machine-specific problem."

## Status today

Same idea. [SITE] (English, 2026-10-22) describes the same assistant (fault reports, manual search, data analysis, work
instructions) now aimed at US plants, with the Knipping reference: [REF] "Knipping reduced mean time to repair (MTTR) by
25%, generated €500K in savings through avoided downtime, and achieved a 95% adoption rate." and "Four German locations
are already onboarded." [FAQ] "In suitable use cases, MTTR can be reduced by up to 25%, filing effort by up to 80%, and
onboarding time by up to 90%." Price today: still not public ("Book a free demo").

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price.** Nothing public at launch or today; the founder's price is the operator's reading (header, item 7), so the
  Price line measures that reading, not the company's price.
- **A per-plant money cost.** Only the global $1.4 trillion is public; the chain cost is the technicians' time instead
  (header).
- **The hours per technician a year.** The sources give one example (6 hours on one breakdown) and shares removed; the
  150 to 300 is the author's arithmetic.
- **A technician's hour.** [BLS]'s median stands in.
- **Who signs, and the purchase steps.** No source names the buyer above the maintenance manager; the plant manager, the
  IT department, the security review and the rollout sign-off are the author's (the SAP or Maximo connection is sourced).
- **How often one technician meets a breakdown.** "Day-to-day" is the team's rhythm; the 2 to 4 working days out of 5 is
  the author's.
- **First-person technician accounts.** No Launch HN or forum thread; the occasions are scripted from [BLOG] (the
  founder's own account of US visits) and [WB]'s two user quotes ("Mit der App kann ich alles direkt dokumentieren und
  muss mir keine Sorgen machen, dass ich etwas vergesse." [With the app I can document everything straight away and
  needn't worry about forgetting something.]).

founder.order_why: The recency question (screen 4) sits between two context screens with the same heading and question (3 and 5), so the context step reads as interrupted and reopened instead of finished in one place.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 repeat the same kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.')
founder.missing: Nothing on the commercial side of a B2B sale. No screen asks the price, or what a technician's time lost to breakdowns costs today. None asks who pays (the plant) or who chooses (the maintenance manager, with the plant manager agreeing), or about purchase friction such as connecting to SAP or Maximo and the IT review. PRIMARY.order_why: It screens me in first (own maintenance team, a line down this week), then shows the idea and asks about it against that same recent breakdown, which flows naturally.

screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a free-typed benefit question and is clearly distinct.

screens.instead: Keep both benefits in the belief: 'For most, their last breakdown would have gone better with it: the line back up sooner, and fixed without waiting for the one person who knows that machine.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what Pairio does better than today's way, this is plainly where I check the benefits Keel drafted from my answer.
screens.why2: "The line back up sooner" and "waiting for the expert" are how we talk on the floor; a technician reads both at once.
screens.why3: A technician who just fixed a breakdown knows whether it took too long and whether they had to wait for the one guy who'd seen it before.
screens.why4: Both rows are distinct and in our words, but the record half of the job is missing: a technician who says "better" because the fault report wrote itself, our -80% filing claim, has nothing to tick.
screens.why5: These are my two advantages, the -25% MTTR and not depending on the one guy, kept as I meant them, with no product name or roles leaking into the rows.
screens.instead: Keep both rows and add: "The fix written up without typing it"

screens.why1: After the fit and what it does better, asking what a technician has to do to take it up is the obvious next thing to check about the tool.
screens.why2: It reads plainly, but "to start using it" plus the hint's "setup" points me at onboarding (installing the app, the SAP or Maximo hookup) when what I mean, and typed, is the extra steps at every breakdown, so I had to read it twice to see which it wanted.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my app asks of a tech at the machine: snap the fault, ask, and speak the fix when the line is back up.
screens.why4: It's a free-text box with one escape chip, "Leave this out of the study", which fits because adoption friction is optional to test.
screens.why5: Keel's belief keeps "speak the fix into the phone when done" but quietly drops my second step, photographing the fault and asking the app first, so only half of what I typed carries through.
screens.instead: What will a technician have to do each time a machine goes down to use it, beyond what they do now? (e.g. take out the phone, photograph the fault and ask, speak the fix when done)

screens.why1: Right after I said what technicians must do to start, Keel shows me its list of those steps to check before it moves on to the test, which is exactly where this belongs.
screens.why2: 'Speak the fix into the phone when done' and 'photograph the fault' are how my technicians and I talk about it, though the intro needlessly repeats the title 'What they'll have to do'.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a tech has to change at the machine, because that is my product's whole mechanism.
screens.why4: Both rows are mine, but the second joins two acts (photograph, then ask), and the plain first step, getting the app on a phone the plant allows on the floor, is missing.
screens.why5: Speaking the fix when done and photographing the fault first are what I typed, and the belief to test is my tested item word for word.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Speak the fix into the phone when done' / 'Photograph the fault before asking' / 'Keep the app on a phone at the machine'; test the first.

screens.why1: Right after I listed what technicians must do to start using Pairio, it makes sense to pick the one effort most likely to stop them, since strangers get only one question on this.
screens.why2: "Speak the fix into the phone when done" and "photograph the fault" are exactly how I describe the workflow, so I can read and pick on first pass.
screens.why3: From my plant visits I know the report after a six-hour fix is the step technicians skip, so I can make this call from what I've seen.
screens.why4: These are the two efforts I named on the previous screen, distinct and in my words; no escape chip is needed because I'm the one choosing.
screens.why5: The belief "Most would speak the fix into the phone when done" is my own adoption step unchanged, and the one-in-three bar is a fair test of it.

screens.why1: After the solution is set and before strangers see the study, asking whether to invite technicians who say yes into a pilot is the obvious last step, and it matches how we actually sell: a scoped pilot on one line.
screens.why2: Two short options and a hint that shows the exact line respondents will see; plain on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect emails from technicians who would try Pairio is my own decision to make.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct, but 'pilot' here means leaving an email to try it, while to me a pilot is a plant running it on one production line for two months, so the label slightly overpromises.
screens.why5: My answer is kept, but the word 'pilot' drifts from my meaning (a plant-level pilot the maintenance manager signs off) toward an individual technician trying the app, and the hint does not say who would sign up.
screens.instead: Ask the technicians who say yes to leave an email to try it? (Yes, ask them / No)

screens.why1: Choosing who will put my questions to technicians belongs right here, once the study is written and before the link goes out.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, voice, credits and text messages into one breath, and it says 'voice' while the interviewer is on video, so I read it twice to work out whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both.
screens.why3: I can play both five-second clips and pick the one I think a technician on a loud shop floor would listen to.
screens.why4: Two distinct named interviewers, each with a sample to hear, a sensible default and the cost the same either way; nothing is missing for this choice.
screens.why5: It names maintenance technicians as I typed them and leaks nothing of Pairio's product into what respondents will hear.
screens.instead: Who should ask maintenance technicians your questions? (Each interviewer appears on video with their own face and voice; every question is also written on screen.) Daphne ▶ Hear · Saskia ▶ Hear

screens.why1: Once I've said who asks my technicians, the obvious next choice is how they answer, voice or tapping, and that matters on a loud plant floor where phones and noise are real constraints.
screens.why2: Most of it is plain, and the loud-room accuracy line speaks straight to my world, but "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" took me a second read: is Daphne's video being made, or is something recording my technicians?
screens.why3: I know how my technicians work, with gloves on, noise, a phone in a pocket and little patience for typing, so I can choose this from what I know.
screens.why4: Voice, read-and-tap and let-them-choose cover the real choices, they are distinct, and each carries its readiness, so I could pick read-and-tap knowing it ships now.
screens.why5: It names my maintenance technicians as I typed them, and nothing of Pairio's product leaks into the answering choices.
screens.instead: How should maintenance technicians answer? — AI interviewer (Daphne asks each question aloud; they talk, type or tap; catches more than 9 in 10 spoken answers even where it's loud · her video is being made, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose (ready when Daphne's video is)

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how technicians answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who actually gets a link, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but each label runs straight into its description with no break ('People I know by name I send each one…'), and 'the Contacts page' names a Keel page I haven't seen in this flow, so the second option takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching technicians through named contacts at the plants we've visited, a list, or a post in a maintenance group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list, and one open link for a group are distinct and cover how I'd reach US technicians; my pick, people by name, fits cleanly.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed about technicians and broken machines; it's only about distribution.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (each gets their own link) · A list from Keel's contact search (Keel makes a link per person; you send them) · A group, one open link (posted where they already are; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside the number that decides it, '4 answered', and every card adds '5 needed to call it', so I know nothing held or failed yet and why.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, only the tally '3 too few · 7 people answered', and on first read I took '3 too few' as three people rather than three cards; it also never says why only 4 of my 7 reached each card.
screens.why_b3: All three names (Compatibility, Relative advantage, Adoption friction) and their lines are word for word what I checked, though the solution statement above them is garbled: it says 'structured fault report' twice and 'gets back an answer' after the report.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' hints that I need at least one more technician through each question, but the page never says so, or says whether the missing 3 of 7 were screened out or could still be counted.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 4 who answered each belief, says plainly that this is too few, and keeps n visible on every card.
screens.instead: Not called yet: only 4 of your 7 technicians reached each of the three beliefs and Keel needs 5. The other 3 had no breakdown in the last 5 working days, so send the study to at least one more technician who just fixed a machine.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right above "5 needed to call it", and the So line ties it to "4 counted, 5 needed", so I know why there is no call yet.
screens.why_b2: The option counts are plain (3 easily, 1 with some steps, 0 against), but the bar reads "3 of 4" next to a "no more than 1 in 3" rule over a five-cell strip with one ghost, and nowhere does it say plainly that all 4 counted were for me, so the bar takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "For most maintenance technicians, a phone was allowed at the machine" are word for word the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic; it does not say that one more clear answer (Travis asked again, or one more technician) would make the call.
screens.why_b5: The verdict line says "4 answered" while the count line says "5 answered · 4 counted", which mislabels counted as answered, though the small group is honestly called "a lean, not a call".
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted said a phone was allowed at the machine (Travis's answer was a guess); one more clear answer makes the call, so ask Travis again or one more technician.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted, 5 needed', so I know where this stands and why.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 and Same 1 over 4 is clear, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads like my own tally rather than the bar (no more than 1 in 3 against), and the doubled '3 3' plus the ghost cell for Travis take a second look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Relative advantage and the line is word for word the belief I checked: the line back up sooner.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't tell me that one more counted technician, or a clear answer from Travis, would settle it, or that Bogdan's planned-work point is worth chasing.
screens.why_b5: It doesn't oversell the lean and it flags the small group and the hypothetical, but the verdict says '4 answered' while the count line says 5 answered with 4 counted, a small mislabel.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 counted technicians say a lot better, 1 says no difference (Bogdan, whose week goes to planned work and short staff). One more clear answer, or re-asking Travis, would decide it; as it stands it leans your way.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted against 5 needed, and the So line repeats the same tie.
screens.why_b2: The bars count each answer over the 4 counted, and the marker sits at 3 of 4, but the ghost cell and a bar written as '3 of 4' while 5 are needed to call it took me a second look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would speak the fix into the phone when done' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that one more counted answer would decide it, or that Travis's end-of-shift quote is the friction I should design around.
screens.why_b5: The verdict line says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', which softly misstates who answered, though the low n and 'a lean, not a call' are said plainly.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 5 answered, 4 counted (Travis's answer was a guess), 3 of 4 would speak the fix in. That leans your way, but one more counted answer decides it, and Travis's 'I want to clock out' says to make the report take seconds at the machine, not at the end of the shift.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Too few to call' with '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' right under it, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together and agree.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the exact names and belief lines I checked on the way in ('the line back up sooner', 'speak the fix into the phone when done').
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need one more answer per line, but the screen never says so, and never says what Bogdan's or Travis's reason means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: n and 'too few' are plain, but Adoption friction's count line says '1 against' while its only quote is Travis marked 'not counted', so I can't tell whose 'against' that is or why it isn't shown.
screens.why_b6: Bogdan's point that his week is eaten by planned work slipping and short staffing, not by missing knowledge, adds to what I wrote; Travis's end-of-a-hot-loud-shift line is close to what my own blog already says.
screens.instead: Too few to call on both: one more technician each. So far the senior tech says staffing, not knowledge, is the drag, and the end-of-shift voice report is where speaking the fix breaks. Ask about the report during the fix, not after.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's obvious why they ask: they want to know I work somewhere that keeps its own maintenance people instead of calling in a contractor.
screens.why2: I'd say 'in-house maintenance' myself, but 'runs its own maintenance team' is plain enough, though 'the US plant' reads a little odd when I've only ever worked at plants here.
screens.why3: I know who fixes the machines where I work, because it's me and the guys on my crew.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it: even with a contractor brought in for some jobs, a plant with its own crew is still a Yes, and a gate needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'US plants that run their own maintenance teams' and doesn't tell me anything about a product.
screens.why6: The stem says fine, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is a clunky way to offer a yes-or-no, and the screener's spoken form is supposed to be just the stem and then 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Does the plant you work at now have its own in-house maintenance crew? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work on an in-house maintenance team, asking whether something went down this week is the obvious next step before asking for the story.
screens.why2: A line going down is shop-floor talk I use every shift, and I can answer it on first read.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether anything went down on my lines in the last week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate should carry no escape, and here there are two: 'I'd rather not say' is not allowed, and 'I can't recall one particular breakdown' does not answer a yes-or-no about whether anything went down.
screens.why5: The founder's case is a machine on the line going down, but 'did a line go down' reads as the whole line stopping, which is narrower, since one machine can be down while the line runs around it.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question ending in 'Yes or no', and I would answer straight away.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a machine on a line you maintain break down? Yes · No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: I just said a line went down this week, so showing me a tool for getting a machine back up and logging the fix is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I know manuals, wiring diagrams, SAP and Maximo, but nobody on the floor says "structured fault report"; we'd call it the work order or the write-up on the ticket.
screens.why3: Looking things up at the machine and closing out the work order after the fix is exactly what I do every breakdown.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The first line "answers and a fault report" doesn't say what the thing is, and the belief line re-lists the how instead of pointing back to it, so it drifts a little from a plain description.
screens.why6: It's long to hear in one go, with the colon list of symptoms, actions and spare parts and a closing belief that repeats the same words, so by the end I'm holding a lot.
screens.instead: Imagine Pairio, an app that answers repair questions at the machine and writes up the work order for you. At the machine you ask by voice or photo, and it searches the manuals, wiring diagrams and past repairs and tells you where the answer came from; after the fix you talk or take photos, and it fills in the work order with symptoms, what you did and parts used, straight into SAP, Maximo or SharePoint. The people building it believe that would get you to the fix faster and leave a real record of it.

screens.why1: Once the idea is something I'd use at a down machine, whether I can even have my phone out on the floor is the first thing I'd want settled.
screens.why2: Plain shop talk; I know straight off whether my phone was allowed out by the press last time it went down.
screens.why3: I know exactly what our plant's phone rule was at that breakdown, and whether a supervisor waved it off.
screens.why4: For a question about being allowed, "Yes, easily" and "Yes, with some steps" read like how hard it was rather than whether it was permitted, and they blur into "only with help or approval".
screens.why5: It asks whether the tool could live where the fix happens, without slipping in any of the founder's product talk beyond the named card.
screens.why6: Short single question with four short options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.instead: Think of your last breakdown. Were you allowed to have your phone out at the machine? Yes; only with a supervisor's okay; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the phone-at-the-machine question, asking whether this thing would have helped on my last breakdown is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; I know which breakdown they mean and what 'better' would look like on the floor.
screens.why3: It's my own last breakdown, so I can weigh whether having answers on hand and a written-up fault report would have helped me get it back up.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse covers it, with no overlap, and 'I can't tell' fits someone who isn't sure from a short card.
screens.why5: It still asks whether the idea would have helped on the actual fix, and 'fault report' is close enough to how we talk about writing up a job, with nothing else leaking.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold in my head, then one escape, so it's easy to answer by ear.

screens.why1: After asking if I could have my phone at the machine and whether it would help, asking if I'd actually talk the fix into it is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Speak the fix into your phone when you finish is how I'd say it myself; nothing in there I'd have to read twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I'd bother talking a fix into my phone after getting a line back up; I do the 'Reset machine.' log entry now, so I know my own habits.
screens.why4: The four cover it, but 'Yes, if it was clearly worth it' and 'Probably not' are both maybes from different sides, and the real catch for me is whether there's time before the next call, not whether it's worth it.
screens.why5: The card names it on purpose and the question only tells me the one thing I'd have to do, no company talk or their words for me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options I can hold after one hearing, one escape said last.
screens.instead: To use Pairio, you'd speak the fix into your phone when you finish. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, if I had a minute before the next call · Probably not · No
